changes.label: Macro Stance
changes.before: South China Morning Post reported: “China’s consumer prices flat in July, while producer deflation persists.” [[n1292]] CNBC reported: “Beijing's anti-involution push won't be too drastic as it could lead to higher unemployment.” [[n1314]] Flat consumer prices and persistent producer deflation are a warning about pricing power, while restraint in the anti-involution campaign reflects the employment cost of abruptly reducing competition. The attractive Chinese equity thesis is therefore selective improvement in business economics, not an assumption that tighter supply automatically restores strong household demand. A company can benefit from reduced destructive discounting while the economy remains uneven. Investors should pay for the operating improvement that can be demonstrated, rather than capitalizing the full ambition of a policy slogan. Distinguish stabilizing supply from rebuilding private demand; both may help earnings, but they operate through different channels and can require very different time horizons.
changes.after: South China Morning Post reported: “China’s consumer prices flat in July, while producer deflation persists.” [[n1292]] Flat July consumer prices and persistent producer deflation keep the focus on companies' ability to earn an adequate margin. The equity opportunity is selective improvement in business economics, rather than an assumption that a policy slogan has already restored household demand. Reduced discounting could help an individual franchise, but it remains a condition to monitor, not an established outcome across the economy. Prefer businesses able to demonstrate customer demand and cash conversion without relying on an immediate, uniform reflation. A stock-market recovery can begin before that broader confirmation arrives, which raises the importance of choosing the actual earnings claim rather than buying every exposure carrying the same national label.
changes.reason: Removed the same-day CNBC anti-involution assessment and the dependent claim that policy restraint reflects a documented employment trade-off. Retained only the eligible July price-release baseline.

changes.label: Credit Check
changes.before: Bloomberg.com reported: “Germany Property Crash Leaves Pension Funds Reeling From Private Credit Losses.” [[n6983]] Losses associated with German property and private credit are a reminder that apparent calm in public markets does not eliminate problems in less liquid assets. A valuation can adjust slowly where transactions are infrequent. For an investor, the important distinction is between assets that can be marked at a comfortable value and assets that can be sold near that value under pressure. Prefer transparent balance sheets and financing terms. Avoid reaching for a little additional yield by accepting a large deterioration in liquidity, particularly if other portfolio holdings already rely on the same benign financing conditions.

Keep that liquidity distinction in the credit allocation without assuming an unverified loss event. Prefer borrowers with cash flow sufficient to service their obligations and financing terms that remain workable when the next refinancing window is less generous. Avoid accepting a large loss of transparency or liquidity for a modest increase in quoted income, especially if other holdings depend on the same benign funding conditions. A comfortable valuation mark and a reliable exit are different protections.

changes.label: Credit Check
changes.before: Bloomberg.com reported: “Credit Spreads Aren't Hiding a Market Timebomb.” [[n3169]] Bloomberg reported: “AT1 Bonds Are So Popular That Spreads Are the Tightest Ever.” [[n3702]] Bloomberg's argument against reading a timebomb into credit spreads and its account of exceptionally popular AT1 debt are compatible only if the security terms are kept in view. Tight spreads can reflect strong demand and still leave a buyer with little compensation for subordination, loss absorption or a change in issuance conditions. A corporate-bond ETF price is not a full spread series, and an attractive quoted yield is not a complete description of the claim. Prefer credit whose underlying borrower can service it without a permanently favorable refinancing market. Reduce where the combination of complexity and illiquidity is being treated as a harmless source of extra income.
changes.after: Bloomberg reported: “AT1 Bonds Are So Popular That Spreads Are the Tightest Ever.” [[n3702]] Popularity and tight spreads do not eliminate the importance of security terms. Strong demand can leave a new buyer with little compensation for subordination, loss absorption or a change in funding conditions. The result is a valuation question, not an automatic prediction of a credit crisis or proof that no risk exists. A corporate-bond ETF price is not a complete spread series, and a quoted yield does not describe every condition attached to the claim. Prefer borrowers able to service debt without permanently favourable refinancing. Reduce exposure where complexity and illiquidity are treated as a harmless route to extra income.
changes.reason: Removed the later credit-timebomb opinion and all attribution to its argument. Retained the earlier-canonical AT1 popularity/spread report and independent reasoning about terms.

changes.label: New / Most Important
changes.before: Bloomberg.com reported: “Tencent’s AI Restraint Shows Risk of Alibaba, JD Food War.” [[n1521]] Tencent's more restrained approach to AI spending supplies a useful contrast with the cash consumed by the delivery battle at other platforms. Restraint should not be interpreted as a rejection of the technology; it can reflect a different assessment of how much spending is needed to earn a customer return. The shareholder benefits when the company can capture demand without matching every competitor's budget. The key question is whether disciplined spending preserves product relevance and monetization. Prefer a measured, profitable deployment over an arms race whose economics depend on competitors eventually becoming less aggressive. Strong revenue growth becomes a more useful investment signal when it is accompanied by evidence that the cost of obtaining it remains under control.
changes.after: CNBC reported: “Chinese tech giant Tencent's quarterly revenue jumps 15% on AI investments, gaming unit boost.” [[n1494]] The reported revenue expansion connects AI investment and gaming to an actual company result. It should not be interpreted as proof that all of the growth comes from AI or that the return on every increment of spending is already established. The investment question is how demand and monetisation translate into cash after the costs of serving customers and defending the franchise. Prefer a company able to demonstrate that bridge, rather than assuming that either the largest budget or the smallest budget wins automatically. More spending can be justified when it earns an adequate return; a higher revenue figure alone does not settle that capital-allocation decision.
changes.reason: Replaced the later Tencent-restraint article with the earlier-canonical CNBC quarterly revenue result; removed every assertion that Tencent had demonstrated a particular spending-restraint strategy.

The South China Morning Post described shipping routes continuing to change despite the truce. [[n1314]] Technology access remains similarly conditional. Reuters reported China cautioning technology firms over Nvidia H20 purchases, citing sources, while the Financial Times described DeepSeek's next model being delayed by an attempt to use Chinese chips. [[n1293]] [[n1436]] A licensing concession therefore cannot be booked automatically as end-customer revenue. Own technology franchises with identifiable domestic monetization, and apply a policy discount where hardware approval, customer acceptance and export permissions all sit between an order and a sale.
changes.reason: Replaced the later Bloomberg newsletter and its Beijing-resistance formulation with Reuters’ already-eligible August 12 source-based caution over H20 purchases. Preserved the separate FT model-delay report and conditional revenue-access analysis.
